clinical_category: Uncal herniation - pupillary and consciousness deterioration
blueprint_topic: Recognition of impending brain herniation from acute neurologic change
stem: A client with rising intracranial pressure develops a newly dilated, nonreactive right pupil and a rapid decline in level of consciousness. Which complication should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Right-sided uncal herniation with compression of adjacent midbrain structures and the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve
options.B: Spinal shock causing transient areflexia below a spinal cord lesion
options.C: Autonomic dysreflexia from bladder distention after high spinal cord injury
options.D: An uncomplicated tension headache without evidence of intracranial mass effect

rationale: A is correct. Current 2026 NCBI/StatPearls guidance explains that uncal herniation occurs when the medial temporal lobe is displaced toward and across the tentorial notch, compressing the midbrain and the ipsilateral third cranial nerve. Characteristic findings include acute loss or decline of consciousness and ipsilateral pupillary dilation; a unilateral dilated pupil may be an early neurologic sign. B and C are spinal-cord syndromes and do not explain the focal pupillary change with worsening intracranial hypertension. D is incompatible with a new fixed/dilated pupil and declining consciousness. The item tests a concrete herniation warning sign rather than merely stating that herniation is life-threatening.
educational_objective: Recognize a new unilateral dilated nonreactive pupil with declining consciousness in a client with rising ICP as a red flag for uncal herniation and urgent neurologic deterioration.
source_version_date: Uncal Herniation current 2026 StatPearls edition; Brain Herniation last updated 2026-02-22; both accessed 2026-08-18
source_locator: NCBI Bookshelf 'Uncal Herniation' → Pathophysiology: the uncus is forced over the tentorial notch, compressing the midbrain and ipsilateral cranial nerve III. History and Physical: characteristic findings include acute loss of consciousness with ipsilateral pupillary dilation; a unilateral dilated pupil may be the first neurologic sign. NCBI Bookshelf 'Brain Herniation' → time-critical red flags include a new dilated nonreactive pupil, rapidly worsening anisocoria, and progressive neurologic decline.
source_claim_supported: Current NCBI/StatPearls content directly supports new ipsilateral pupillary dilation/nonreactivity and declining consciousness as warning findings of uncal herniation from rising intracranial pressure.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation client-needs subcategory (11–17% of items); this item tests recognition of a life-threatening acute neurologic complication and deterioration in physiologic function.
correction_summary: Total clinical rebuild. The original generic AANN item only stated that brain herniation can compress vital structures and cause death, duplicating nearby increased-ICP content. The final item uses current 2026 StatPearls guidance and tests a specific, clinically actionable uncal-herniation pattern: new unilateral pupillary dilation/nonreactivity with declining consciousness.
audit_findings: The original AANN root URL did not provide an exact current locator and the construct was too generic to justify a separate item.
Current 2026 StatPearls directly links uncal herniation to ipsilateral cranial-nerve-III compression, pupillary dilation, and declining consciousness.
The final construct is distinct from V2-Q1977 (earlier increased-ICP signs) and V2-Q1978 (Cushing response).
No unsupported ICP threshold or timing rule was required in the keyed answer.
Independent adversarial second pass found one uniquely correct diagnosis, no second defensible option, no cueing, and no unresolved conflict.
